To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) perceived workload is not a significant factor in inducing a deep learning strategy; 2) a lack of information in a task increases surface learning strategies; 3) a lack of feedback in a task decreases a deep approach to a task and increases a deep approach to the course.

(a) a perceived lack of task complexity is a discouraging and a perceived lack of workload is an encouraging factor for inducing a surface approach to learning, (b) a perceived lack or excess of task complexity is an encouraging and discouraging factor for a deep approach to study, and (c) perceived workload has a neutral influence on the approach to study.
a lack of information is consistently a discouraging factor, whereas the workload and task complexity do not have a consistent influence on the students' learning approaches.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of workload and task-complexity on students' approaches towards learning.
the question as to how workload and task complexity influence the learning approach of students in higher education.
the question as to whether perceived workload and perceived lack of information are factors which discourage or encourage a deep learning approach to learning in higher education.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the perceived lack of information in the tasks is a discouraging and consistent factor for inducing a surface approach to learning.
the perceived lack of information in a learning task is a discouraging and negative factor for inducing a deeper approach to learn.
perceived workload does not have an impact on students' approaches, whereas perceived task complexity is a discouraging and encouraging factor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the perceived lack of information in the learning environment is the most discouraging factor for a deep approach to studying.
the relationship between perceived workload, perceived task complexity and students' approaches towards learning are more complex than previously thought.
perceived workload is not related to the students' approaches to learn and perceived task complexity is a discouraging variable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
students are not always able to perceive workload and task complexity as a learning opportunity.
perceived task complexity is a more important factor than perceived workload for inducing students' approaches to learn.
students who perceive a lack of information are more likely to use a surface approach to learning, regardless of the induced task complexity or perceived workload.
